findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async`, so callers will `await` it expecting it to yield control while the HTTP request is in flight. But `requests.get` is fully synchronous: it blocks the thread running the event loop until the billing service responds or the 5-second timeout fires. Every other coroutine on that loop — including unrelated requests being served — is frozen for that whole window, so a slow `billing.internal` turns into loop-wide latency rather than a single slow request.

The file already imports `httpx` and the sibling `fetch_plan` demonstrates the intended pattern. Use an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`, e.g. accept a client parameter as `fetch_plan` does, or `async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as client: response = await client.get(...)`. If a synchronous client genuinely must be used, wrap it in `asyncio.to_thread(...)`. The new `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

No test exists for this function, so nothing would fail if the function were rewritten incorrectly, returned malformed data, or continued blocking the event loop under load. Since this is the exact behavior the PR is meant to add for showing quota, a test asserting on the parsed return value (with the HTTP call mocked) would catch both logic regressions and confirm intended behavior.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the target URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. `tenant_id` is unvalidated and untyped, so any string reaches the URL path verbatim. If the caller passes a value taken from the request (path segment, query param, or JSON body), an attacker controls part of a URL aimed at an internal, network-trusted host and can reach endpoints other than `/limits/...` — e.g. `..%2f..%2fadmin/keys`, or appending `?`/`#` to truncate or rewrite the rest of the path and inject query parameters. The blast radius is whatever else `billing.internal` exposes to callers that are inside the network perimeter.

Fix: validate/constrain `tenant_id` before use (assert it matches an expected shape such as a UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`), and/or pass it through an escaping layer rather than string interpolation — e.g. `requests.get("https://billing.internal/limits/" + quote(str(tenant_id), safe=""))`, or build the URL from a template with an explicitly encoded segment. The same treatment applies to `fetch_plan` on line 6, which has the identical pattern.

If `_client.send` is interrupted by Ctrl-C or during interpreter shutdown, this handler converts that into a normal `return None` and the process keeps going as if nothing happened — a worker that cannot be shut down cleanly. Narrow this to `except Exception:` so only ordinary failures are absorbed.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` into `current` (line 15), then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (line 18), then writes the absolute value `current + cost` (line 19) — all without acquiring `_lock`, which every other mutation of `_counters` holds (line 9).

Two concrete failures:

1. **Limit bypass.** Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current = 999`, both evaluate `999 + 1 > 1000` as false, and both proceed — the tenant is charged past `LIMIT`. With N concurrent callers the overshoot is unbounded.
2. **Lost update.** Line 19 assigns rather than increments from the current value. If `consume()` (line 10) or another `try_consume` writes while this coroutine is suspended at line 18, that write is silently discarded when line 19 stores the stale `current + cost`. The counter can go backwards, which permanently weakens the limiter for that tenant.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the same lock, and by incrementing from a freshly read value rather than a stale local:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

Note that the `await` must not remain inside the critical section unless it is genuinely needed; `asyncio.sleep(0)` here only serves to widen the race window.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses _lock, so the rate limit can be exceeded at will

There is no test in this diff that would catch two concurrent try_consume calls both passing the limit check and pushing the total over LIMIT. A single-threaded or sequential test would pass even if the race allows tenants to exceed the rate limit, which is the entire point of this feature.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding failed inserts
findings.body:

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates failures across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, meaning the second invocation returns the failures from the first invocation plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results, and may re-dispatch to recipients that already succeeded.

Use `attempted=None` and initialise inside the body:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
```

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a pure rename
findings.body:
This PR is described as a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. Every other function in the hunk is byte-identical apart from its name, so this is almost certainly unintended.

The behavioural difference is reachable and financially meaningful: a line with `remainder_cents == 0.5` previously rounded up to 1 cent and now rounds down to 0. Half-up is the conventional rule for currency rounding, and exactly-0.5 remainders are common (any odd number of half-cent splits), so this will silently shift totals by a cent on a non-trivial fraction of lines and may break reconciliation against previously-stored values.

Restore `>=` unless the operator change is deliberate — in which case it belongs in a separate, documented commit with tests covering the 0.5 boundary.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` but slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, returning only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because the next page's start still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE`, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — a caller iterating pages until an empty/short result will silently lose one record out of every `PAGE_SIZE`, and short-page-means-last-page logic will terminate early on a full final page. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match `page_of` on line 6.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge()`, but `billing/gateway.py` states explicitly that the call is NOT idempotent and that each call creates a new charge. Retries only fire on failure, and the failures that matter most here are exactly the ambiguous ones: a timeout, connection reset, or 5xx returned after the gateway has already accepted the POST. In those cases the retry issues a second and third `/charges` request and the customer is charged two or three times, with no way for the caller to detect it.

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge attempt (outside the retried function, so all attempts share it), pass it through to `charge()`, and only then wrap in `retry`. If passing a key is not possible yet, remove the retry from this path and let the caller decide, or restrict retries to errors that provably occurred before the request was sent (e.g. connection-establishment failures) rather than all exceptions.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above: `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat, so the retry there is correct. The same decorator is not safe on the write path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

The retry decorator on `charge_card` will retry on failure without this safeguard, risking duplicate charges. The function needs a docstring that documents this hazard, or the implementation must pass an Idempotency-Key header (neither is present).

The new @retry(attempts=3) decorator will retry this non-idempotent call on failure with no idempotency key threaded through, meaning a transient network error after the gateway processed the charge could cause up to 3 real charges. There is no test in this diff verifying that retries do not produce duplicate charges, nor a test asserting an idempotency key is passed/reused across retry attempts. A test exercising a failure-then-success scenario against charge_card and asserting the underlying charge() call count or resulting charge count would catch this.

`upsert` explicitly documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and states that it does not normalise them — a term differing only by case creates a second posting list that queries (which do lower-case) will never match. `article.title.split()` yields the title's words verbatim, so any capitalised word (which in a title is most of them, including the first) is indexed under a posting list no query can reach. The article indexes without error and is silently unfindable by those terms.

Normalise before the call, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})`. Stripping punctuation is likely needed too, since `split()` leaves trailing commas/periods attached to words.

findings.title: Referer header is logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token
findings.body:
The removed branch existed specifically because `Referer` can carry credentials: `token_authenticated_url` hands out notebook URLs as `{base}?token={token}`, and the browser replays that full URL in the `Referer` header of every subresource request. Writing `request.headers["Referer"]` straight into the log means any 5xx produces a log line containing a live auth token, which is then readable by anyone with log access (operators, log shipping pipelines, support bundles) and grants full session access.

Restore the per-header sanitisation before building the dict, e.g. keep `value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` for `Referer` (and consider the same for any other URL-bearing header you add later). If the goal was to reduce branching, do the scrubbing in a small helper rather than dropping it.

Note also that `extra_param_keys` appears to have no remaining use in this function after the removal, which is a signal the sanitisation was dropped rather than relocated.

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no test guarding the behavior
findings.body: The change deletes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously stripped the auth token from the Referer header before logging. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts logged headers are scrubbed or unscrubbed, so this regression — tokens now landing verbatim in logs — would pass silently through any existing test suite. A test that constructs a request with a token in the Referer header and asserts the logged output does not contain the raw token would catch this.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref skips URL validation instead of blocking the attribute
findings.body:
The branch at line 6 is a *validation* dispatch, not an allowlist: attributes matched here are forwarded to `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, and anything not matched falls through to whatever the function returns below (evidently `true`/allowed, since `href`/`src` need an explicit check to be restricted). Removing `xlinkhref` therefore does not "drop" the attribute — it lets `xlink:href` render with its value completely unchecked, so author-supplied markdown such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` reaches the DOM with an executable scheme. `xlink:href` is the classic SVG equivalent of `href` and is exactly the case the `unsafeLinkPrefix` list (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`) exists to stop.

If the intent is genuinely to stop supporting the attribute, it must be rejected (`return false`) or excluded from the rendered attribute set elsewhere — not removed from the scheme check. Otherwise restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the default branch is and is no longer scheme-filtered. Adversary: any end user who can submit markdown (the file header states rendered attributes come from user-submitted markdown). What they control: the attribute value, e.g. ``. What they get: script execution in the origin of every viewer of that content — stored XSS, session/token theft. Note the PR description says it drops "rarely used SVG attributes we do not need" — but this line is not an allowlist of which attributes are rendered, it is the list of attributes that get URL validation. Removing an entry here does not stop `xlink:href` being emitted; it only stops it being checked. If the intent really is to not support `xlink:href`, it must be removed from the attribute allowlist (or explicitly rejected), not from the validation branch. Otherwise restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` here.

findings.title: No test guards validateProp's xlinkhref handling
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the attribute check in validateProp, meaning xlink:href values will no longer be routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed and will presumably fall through to a default (likely permissive) path. There is no test file in this change exercising validateProp with attribute 'xlinkhref', so a regression here — intentional or not — would not be caught by any existing suite. If this behavior is wrong (i.e., xlinkhref should still be sanitised), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller contract
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is now passed downstream without any identifier check. The retrieved `DAO.buildPath` documents the opposite contract: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." It then calls `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `filepath.Join` applies `Clean`, so a project value such as `../../etc` resolves *above* `d.Folder` rather than being contained by it — the PR description's claim that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" is not true of `filepath.Join`.

Also note the surviving check on line 4 only compares the query parameter against `parameters.Project` when the latter is non-empty; when the path parameter is absent, the unvalidated query value is the sole source of the project name, so nothing else constrains it.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (or move an equivalent validation into `buildPath` and update its doc comment) before the value can reach the filesystem layer.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets query param reach filepath.Join unvalidated

findings.title: Removed project-name validation lacks a regression test
findings.body: The removed call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) previously rejected malformed/malicious project names supplied via the query parameter before they reach buildPath, which per the DAO docs performs no validation itself and relies on callers to have validated names. Removing this check changes behavior (any string, including path-traversal sequences like '../../etc', is now accepted) but there is no test in this diff exercising list() with an invalid/traversal-style projectQueryParameter to confirm the new behavior is intentional or to catch a future regression if the check is restored incorrectly elsewhere.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`contentLength` on this path comes from the request's declared Content-Length header and is passed straight into `Reserve(...)`, which commits the allocation up front rather than growing as bytes actually arrive. A client can declare a very large part size (e.g. many GiB) and send few or no bytes, and the server will still reserve the memory — one small request per unit of RAM, repeatable concurrently. The previous incremental growth bounded the allocation by bytes genuinely received.

Validate before reserving: clamp to the maximum permitted part size (and reject anything above it with the appropriate S3 error) and only reserve `min(contentLength, cap)`. The allocation should never exceed what the server is willing to buffer regardless of what the client claims.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Part buffer pre-allocated from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test exercises Reserve(contentLength) behavior or edge cases
findings.body: The change adds Reserve(contentLength) to pre-allocate the multipart buffer based on Content-Length. There is no test verifying this path, so a regression (e.g. Reserve panicking or misbehaving when contentLength is negative/unknown, such as chunked transfer encoding where Content-Length may be -1) would not be caught. If the surrounding test suite for this file already lacks unit tests for uploadPart, this is consistent with existing coverage and only worth a light note.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression only downgraded to `http` when the caller explicitly set `request.meta['is_secure'] = False`; any other state (key absent, `None`, `True`) yielded `https`. The new expression is not equivalent: `request.meta.get("is_secure")` returns `None` for the common case where the key was never set, which is falsy, so the scheme becomes `http`.

That means every S3 download that does not explicitly opt into `is_secure=True` now transmits over an unencrypted connection to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com`, carrying the AWS request signature/credentials headers in cleartext. This is a silent, repo-wide default change, not a simplification.

If the goal is a single ternary, preserve the original default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme downgraded from HTTPS to plaintext HTTP
findings.body:
The previous expression only chose `http` when the caller explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = False`; any other state (key absent, `None`) yielded `https`. The new ternary treats absent/`None`/falsy identically to an explicit opt-out, so every request that does not positively set `is_secure` to a truthy value is now built as `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` on line 6.

The two expressions are only equivalent when `is_secure` is always present and boolean; for the common case of it being unset they differ, and the difference is loss of transport encryption.

Restore fail-secure behaviour, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `is_secure = request.meta.get("is_secure", True)` before the ternary, so that HTTPS remains the default and plaintext requires an explicit opt-out.

findings.title: No test covers default scheme when is_secure is unset
findings.body: The change flips the default behavior: previously, when 'is_secure' was absent from request.meta, the scheme defaulted to 'https' (since only an explicit False triggered 'http'). Now, absence of 'is_secure' defaults to 'http' (since get() returns None, which is falsy). This is a meaningful security-relevant behavior change (default now sends requests in plaintext unless is_secure is explicitly truthy), but no test in this diff verifies scheme selection for any of the three cases: is_secure=True, is_secure=False, or is_secure absent/None. Without such a test, a regression reintroducing or altering this default would not be caught.

findings.title: DELETE now requests "push" access, bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
The removed switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the action `"delete"`. The new condition only special-cases GET/HEAD, so DELETE falls into the `else` branch and produces `action = "push"`. The authorization config documents three deliberately distinct actions — "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones" — so any principal granted only `push` on a repository can now issue DELETE requests and pass the access check. Conversely, a principal granted only `delete` (no push) will be denied. Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: No test guards DELETE→action mapping change
findings.body: The new logic maps http.MethodDelete to "push" (since it's neither GET nor HEAD), whereas the old code mapped it to a distinct "delete" action per the documented three-action model in pkg/api/config/config.go. This is a behavior change to authorization action derivation, but the diff includes no test asserting the action produced for a DELETE request. If this mapping is wrong (e.g. should still be "delete"), nothing in the current test suite would fail.

findings.title: Public auth behavior change undocumented in code
findings.body: The logic change that treats DELETE requests as "push" rather than a separate "delete" action should be documented in a comment, particularly since it contradicts the documented three-action model elsewhere. Without explanation, future maintainers may assume the DELETE case was accidentally removed.

findings.title: Default action for unlisted methods flipped from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, etc.) to `"pull"`. The new negated condition sends all of them to `"push"`. This is stricter rather than looser, but it is a behaviour change that was not part of the stated intent and will reject e.g. CORS preflight OPTIONS requests from pull-only clients. If the stricter default is intended, it deserves to be explicit; otherwise keep the non-mutating methods on "pull".

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole shared cache, including the just-written entry
findings.body:
When `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries the function calls `_CACHE.clear()`, discarding every cached tenant rather than evicting one. Two consequences: (1) the entry written on line 10 is thrown away immediately, so a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` followed by `get_tenant(x)` gets `None` back from line 5 even though the fetch succeeded; (2) every other caller of `get_tenant` silently loses its cached data whenever any caller happens to cross the threshold, turning a single refresh into a full cache stampede against `_fetch`. Prefer a bounded eviction policy (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` popitem/LRU, or `functools.lru_cache`) that removes the oldest entry, and do the eviction before inserting so the fresh value survives.

The check-then-act on lines 11-12 is also not atomic: with concurrent callers two threads can both observe `len(_CACHE) > 1000` and both clear, or a clear can land between another thread's write on line 10 and its read via `get_tenant`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Cache eviction clears the entire shared cache on overflow

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's cache update and eviction logic is untested
findings.body: The new function writes to _CACHE and clears it when it exceeds 1000 entries, but no test exercises either behavior. If the eviction threshold were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, or clearing too aggressively/never), or if the cache write were dropped, nothing in this diff would fail. Add tests that verify: (1) calling get_tenant_fresh populates _CACHE with the fetched value, (2) the cache is cleared once size exceeds 1000, and (3) the returned value matches the fetched tenant.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag `--workers`
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as a CLI flag on line 7, but the code on line 6 of cli.py has renamed this flag to `--concurrency`. A user reading the README will attempt to use the old flag name, which no longer exists. Update the documentation to match the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed `--workers` flag

findings.title: Flag rename breaks existing callers and `args.workers` consumers
findings.body: Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` changes two contracts at once: the accepted command-line surface (existing scripts, CI jobs and container entrypoints passing `--workers N` will now fail with `unrecognized arguments`), and argparse's derived destination, so any code doing `args.workers` raises `AttributeError` and must be updated to `args.concurrency`. If the intent is only to align the user-facing name with the internal one, keep the old spelling working, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4, dest="concurrency")`, or add a separate hidden `--workers` alias that warns on use. If a hard break is intended, this should be called out as breaking and every reader of `args.workers` updated in the same change. No consumer code was retrieved, so I cannot confirm which call sites exist.

findings.title: No test verifies the renamed --concurrency flag is parsed
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency with no accompanying test change. If a script or wrapper still passes --workers, argparse will now fail with an unrecognized-argument error, or if the rename is reverted, nothing here would catch it. Add or update a test asserting `parser().parse_args(['--concurrency', '2']).concurrency == 2`.

findings.title: Docstring does not match changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day strings to call counts. A caller reading the docstring would expect an integer and would break when receiving a dict. Update the docstring to document the new return type: a dict with day keys and integer call-count values.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; docstring and callers not updated
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `f"{usage} calls"`, summing across accounts) will now silently misbehave or raise. No caller updates are present in this one-file change. Either keep a total-returning entry point and add the breakdown under a new name, or update every call site in the same change. At minimum, line 2's docstring still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer" and is now wrong.

findings.title: Behaviour change from int to dict has no test coverage
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test in the diff verifies the new shape (keys, values, grouping) or that callers were updated accordingly. If the query, grouping, or key format were wrong, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body:
The docstring on line 6 documents the parameter as 'page_size: how many invoices to return' but the function signature on line 1 has renamed this parameter to 'limit'. A caller reading the docstring will see a parameter name that does not exist in the actual function signature, causing confusion and potential errors when calling the function.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old `page_size` parameter

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` breaks callers that pass it by keyword
findings.body: `page_size` is a public positional-or-keyword parameter of `list_invoices`. Any existing call site written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime rather than failing at import time. Either grep and update all call sites in the same change, or accept both names for a deprecation period (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping the old name onto the new one with a warning). No caller code was retrieved here, so the number of affected sites is unverified.

findings.title: Signature rename to list_invoices has no accompanying test
findings.body: list_invoices' parameter was renamed from page_size to limit, which breaks any caller using it as a keyword argument. No test file is included in this diff, and nothing shown verifies that list_invoices still works correctly with the renamed parameter or that call sites were updated. If the rename introduced a mismatch (e.g. a caller still passing page_size=...), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a package module
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this file is explicitly relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not against the `requests` package, so under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import` enabled) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — i.e. the whole library fails to import. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, yet the surviving `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either restore the helper or finish removing `old_request` along with it.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor. Callers using `session.get(url, timeout=5)` or `verify=False` will silently get unbounded/verified behaviour instead of an error — a silent behaviour change is worse than a `TypeError`. It also no longer merges session-level state (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.config`), so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare one. Either thread these through to the prepared request/adapter or drop them from the signature until they are wired up.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send, and close() no longer releases anything
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a brand-new `HTTPAdapter` on every call, so each request gets its own connection pool and no connection is ever reused — the pooling behaviour the `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize` config still advertises is gone, and nothing ever clears those pools (the adapter is dropped unreferenced after each send). In parallel, `close()` is now `pass`, so `with requests.Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` no longer free sockets. Hold one adapter on the `Session` (created in `__init__`) and have `close()` close it. Note also that `self.poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager()` were public attributes/hooks; any code or subclass that referenced them now breaks with `AttributeError`.

findings.title: Refactor removes tested behaviour with no test to catch regressions
findings.body: close() previously cleared the PoolManager to release pooled connections; it is now `pass`, silently dropping that behaviour. Session.send() now delegates to a brand-new HTTPAdapter.send() instead of request.send(), and request() is a rewritten duplicate of old_request(). None of these changes are covered by any test in this diff, so if close() should still release resources, if the new request() mis-populates a field (e.g. verify/cert/timeout/stream are dropped entirely versus old_request), or if HTTPAdapter.send() behaves differently from request.send(), nothing would fail.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but silently dropped before send
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still advertises `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149), but the body never reads them: it copies method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto `req`, calls `req.prepare()`, and then `self.send(prep)` — which constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no TLS configuration at all (lines 365-366). Any caller that passes `verify='/path/to/ca-bundle.pem'` or `cert=(...)`, or that set a session-level default, now gets whatever the adapter's built-in default is, with no error and no warning.

The adversary here is anyone in a position to intercept the connection (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream proxy, DNS/BGP attacker). They control the network path only; if `HTTPAdapter.send` defaults to not verifying (or to the system default rather than the caller's pinned bundle), they get to terminate TLS and read/modify request bodies and credentials that the caller explicitly asked to be protected.

Either thread `verify`/`cert` through to `send()`/the adapter, or remove them from the signature so the failure is loud rather than silent.

findings.title: Top-level `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` instead of relative import
findings.body:
Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...` on lines 18-19). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolved against `sys.path`, not the package. On Python 3 this raises ImportError; on Python 2 it works only by accident of implicit relative imports. Where it does resolve via `sys.path`, the entry that wins can be the interpreter's script directory or working directory, so a stray or attacker-dropped `adapters.py` in the application's directory would substitute the object that performs every HTTP send for this library — a local attacker who can write a file next to the entry script gets to see and rewrite all outbound traffic.

Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking its callers
findings.body:
On a malformed `Cookie` header the except branch sets `self._cookies = None` and that value is cached by the `hasattr` guard, so the property permanently returns `None` for that request. The docstring promises "a dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects", and both remaining callers assume that: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable) and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (AttributeError). The old code called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which left `_cookies` a real `SimpleCookie`. Since an `HTTPRequest` cannot clear response cookies, the correct fallback here is to reset to an empty container: `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()`. Note this is attacker-controllable — any client can send a garbage Cookie header and turn every `get_cookie` call into a 500.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header sets _cookies=None, crashing all cookie readers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed without an alias to request.cookies
No test coverage for moved/changed cookies property behavior
findings.body: The cookies property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior silently changed: on a malformed Cookie header it now sets self._cookies = None (httpserver.py:523) instead of calling clear_all_cookies() as the original web.py version did. This means request.cookies could return None instead of an empty SimpleCookie, which would break callers like clear_all_cookies() (iterating .iterkeys() on None) and get_cookie() (checking 'name in self.request.cookies'). No test exercises a malformed Cookie header, get_cookie, or clear_all_cookies against this new property, so this behavior change and the potential None-related crash would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: missing strip() on split segments
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that every real client emits: `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. `" boundary=----abc".partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop finishes without breaking, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the for/else logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" for perfectly valid requests. The previous code used `'boundary=' in content_type` / `split('boundary=', 1)[1]`, which was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression that disables multipart form/file uploads.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider `k.lower()` plus stripping surrounding quotes from `v`, since parameter names are case-insensitive and boundaries may be quoted).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Boundary parameter never matches: missing strip() on split fields

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing when boundary isn't last
findings.body: The change fixes a bug where 'boundary' was assumed to be the last parameter in the Content-Type header. There is no test in this diff exercising a Content-Type string like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8' (boundary not last) to confirm the parser now correctly extracts the boundary and parses the body. Without such a test, a future regression back to the old split-based logic (or an equivalent bug) would not be caught.

findings.title: get_host() authority parsing diverges from urlparse (host confusion / SSRF bypass)
findings.body:
`get_host()` splits the URL on `://`, then `/`, then `@`, then `:` — but it never removes the query (`?`) or fragment (`#`) before locating the authority, and it takes the *first* `@` rather than the last.

Consequence, for `http://google.com?@evil.com/`:
- line 92-93 splits on `/`, leaving `google.com?@evil.com`
- line 94-95 splits on the `@`, yielding host `evil.com`

`urlparse('http://google.com?@evil.com/').hostname` is `google.com`. The same divergence occurs with `#`, e.g. `http://google.com#@evil.com/`. Since the host returned here is what the pool manager uses to choose the connection target (and what per-host credentials/pools are keyed on), an application that vets a user-supplied URL with `urlparse`/`urlsplit` against an allowlist and then hands the original string to urllib3 will connect to a host it never approved.

Fix: cut the URL at the first `?` or `#` before parsing the authority, and use `rsplit('@', 1)` for userinfo — or delegate to `urlsplit` and only keep the "simplified" behaviour for scheme-less inputs.

Adversary: anyone who can supply a URL to such an application (webhook target, avatar-fetch, link preview). They control the whole URL string. They get requests issued to an internal or attacker-chosen host while the app believes it is talking to the allowlisted one.

findings.title: New util.py logic (make_headers, get_host) has no visible tests
findings.body: make_headers and get_host contain branching logic (accept_encoding type handling, URL parsing with scheme/port/auth extraction, error raising on bad port) that is lifted into a new module but not accompanied by any test file in this diff. If get_host mis-parses a URL, or make_headers builds the wrong header set, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the URL, so the exception text is literally `Failed to parse: %s`. Anyone debugging a bad host string gets no information about which URL failed. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url argument, since `url` has already been chopped by the scheme/path/auth splits above — passing the pre-split value would be more useful still).

findings.title: accept_encoding type check uses `str`, silently discarding other string types
findings.body: The `else` branch overwrites whatever the caller passed with `'gzip,deflate'`. That is intended for `True`, but it also swallows any string-like value that is not exactly `str` (e.g. a `unicode` literal under Python 2, which this module explicitly supports given the `six` import) and any non-list sequence such as a tuple. The caller's encoding preference is then silently replaced rather than honoured or rejected. Consider `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` and widening the join branch to `(list, tuple)`.

findings.title: No test exercises sorting by the "status" column
findings.body: SORTABLE now supports created_at, amount, and status, and direction toggling. Tests cover amount+asc and the default (created_at/desc via test_lists_newest_first), plus rejection of invalid sort/direction. But no test calls list_invoices with sort="status", so a bug in that column mapping (e.g. wrong DB column name) would not be caught.

findings.title: No test verifies describe() output after removing casts
findings.body: The change alters how event.x and event.code are accessed (via narrowing instead of explicit casts). If the union narrowing were broken by a future refactor (e.g., changing property names or discriminant), nothing in this diff would catch it since no test file is included. Add or confirm a test asserting describe() returns the expected string for both 'click' and 'key' event kinds.

findings.title: location attribute now stores URL object, not string as documented
findings.body:
The `HTTPMove.location` attribute is documented in `docs/web_reference.rst` as storing the location 'as the string it was constructed with', and the documentation notes that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. However, this diff changes the attribute to store a `URL` object instead of a string. This breaks the documented contract and will cause application code relying on string operations to fail.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently void string-based redirect checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `self.location` now a URL object, breaking documented string contract

findings.title: No test guards `self.location` remaining a string
findings.body: The docs state `HTTPMove.location` is exposed "as the string it was constructed with" and application code calls `str.startswith` on it. This diff changes `self.location` to be assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string, which is a behavior/type change. There is no test asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or checking `.startswith` usage on `location`, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Single `if` wait lets readany() return b'' before EOF
findings.body:
`_wait()`'s own docstring states that the waiter "is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake (chunk boundary, or a `feed_data`/`feed_eof` that leaves the buffer empty), control falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns `b''` even though `self._eof` is still False.

Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), so this silently truncates reads. Restore the loop:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Spurious wake now returns empty body, enabling attacker-framed truncation

findings.title: No test exercises repeated wakeups with still-empty buffer
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, removing the retry loop for spurious wakeups. The docstring for `_wait` explicitly states 'the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived.' This diff removes that re-check/retry behavior for `readany`, but no test in the diff (or apparently in the existing suite) simulates a feed_data/feed_eof wakeup that leaves the buffer still empty, which is exactly the scenario this change alters. If such a wakeup occurs in production, `readany` would now return prematurely (via `_read_nowait(-1)` on an empty buffer) instead of continuing to wait, and nothing would catch this regression.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module loading on Python 3
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level module. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` only resolves under Python 2's implicit relative import rules; on Python 3 it raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` (or, worse, silently binds an unrelated top-level `adapters` package if one happens to be installed). Since this is a module-level import, every `import requests` that pulls in `sessions` fails. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Top-level `adapters` import allows sys.path module hijacking
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves unambiguously to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path`, which for a script-launched process includes the script's directory and, in many invocations (e.g. `python -c`, `python -m`, interactive), the current working directory. Any writable directory that appears earlier on `sys.path` than site-packages lets a local user drop an `adapters.py` whose module-level code executes with the privileges of every process that imports `requests.sessions` — and whose `HTTPAdapter` then mediates all HTTP traffic (TLS verification, proxies, connection pooling) for that process.

Adversary: any local principal who can write into the working directory or another early `sys.path` entry (shared build dirs, world-writable tmp used as cwd, a repo checked out by CI). What they control: the entire contents of the shadowing `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code execution in-process plus full control of the HTTP transport adapter.

Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or the absolute `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`). Note this is also a hard `ImportError` under Python 3, where implicit relative imports were removed.

findings.title: Import change to adapters module is untested and would break at import time
findings.body: The import statement was changed from an explicit relative import ('.adapters') to an implicit relative import ('adapters'). Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with 'from __future__ import absolute_import' enabled, or when the package isn't on sys.path directly), this changes the import from a package-relative import to an absolute import that will raise ImportError, breaking the entire module at load time. There is no test in this diff, and if any existing test suite imports requests.sessions, it would fail on collection — but if no test currently imports this module directly, nothing catches the regression.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented and implemented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py` lines 5-9: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that" / `if self._cookies is None: return None`). The removed guard was precisely that allowance. With the guard gone, `name in None` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed Cookie header, turning a previously well-behaved `default` return into a 500. Either restore the `is not None` check, or change the property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` and update its docstring and all other consumers accordingly.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Code contradicts documented cookies contract
findings.body: The change removes the None check on `self.request.cookies`, but the documented contract in `httpserver.py` states that `cookies` can be `None` when the Cookie header cannot be parsed. The new code `if name in self.request.cookies:` will raise a `TypeError` if `cookies` is `None`, violating the documented behavior that "every consumer has to allow for that." Either restore the None check or update the cookies property documentation to guarantee it never returns None.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (see `tornado/httpserver.py`) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". Dropping the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully attacker-controlled and requiring no authentication. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by every handler that calls `get_cookie` — including the secure-cookie/XSRF paths that run before authorisation. Result: an unhandled exception and a 500 on any request the attacker chooses, i.e. a trivially reproducible availability problem, and potentially a stack trace in logs/debug output.

Either restore the guard, or change the source so `cookies` yields an empty mapping instead of `None` for unparseable headers (and update all other consumers accordingly).

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks multipart boundary detection
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that, for the conventional header form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz`, begin with a space (RFC 9110 allows OWS after the `;`). The previous `field.strip()` removed that whitespace before `partition("=")`, so `k` was exactly `"boundary"`. Without it, `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the multipart body is silently discarded — file uploads and form fields vanish with no error raised. The strip also trimmed trailing whitespace/CR from the value, which is likewise lost. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (or strip `k` and `v` individually).

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes multipart boundary parsing whitespace-dependent
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the conventional leading space (`" boundary=abc"`). Previously `field.strip()` normalised that before `partition("=")`; now `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, so `_parse_mime_body` is never reached for the standard, RFC-conformant form of the header and the request body is silently discarded (no error, empty arguments/files).

Security consequence, beyond the plain breakage: the attacker is any HTTP client; what they control is the whitespace and ordering inside their own `Content-Type` header; what they get is control over which parser sees which body. Two concrete shapes:

- `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=A` — an upstream proxy, WAF or upload scanner parses the body with boundary `A` and passes it; Tornado parses nothing, so any downstream code that treats "no such field" as a default rather than a rejection diverges from what was inspected.
- `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B` — a compliant intermediary takes the first parameter (`A`), Tornado now skips it and takes `B`, so the two see completely different sets of fields and files from the same byte stream. That is a straightforward upload/content-filter bypass wherever Tornado sits behind an inspecting hop.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`. Note also that the PR description says the removed strip was "a redundant strip on the parameter value" — it was applied to the whole parameter (affecting the key), not to the value, so the stated justification does not hold.

findings.title: No test covers whitespace-sensitive boundary parsing after removing strip()
findings.body: The change drops `.strip()` before `partition("=")` on each semicolon-separated field of the Content-Type header. Previously `field.strip().partition("=")` would tolerate a leading space before `boundary` (e.g. "multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz", which is the common formatting with a space after the semicolon). Now `field.partition("=")` on " boundary" yields k == " boundary" (with leading space), which no longer equals "boundary", so the `if k == "boundary" and v:` check fails and the boundary is silently not found. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite) that sends a Content-Type header with a space after the semicolon to catch this regression.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The `% url` argument was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the string, so the raised exception reads literally `Failed to parse: %s` and no longer identifies the offending URL. If the goal was to shorten the message, pass the value directly, e.g. `raise LocationParseError(url)` or `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`. As written, callers and logs that relied on the URL appearing in `str(exc)` lose that information, and the stray `%s` will look like a formatting bug in any user-facing traceback.

findings.title: No test covers the error message for invalid port parsing
findings.body: The change drops the `% url` argument from the format string, so `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` would raise with a literal '%s' instead of the actual URL. Nothing in the diff or referenced tests exercises `parse_url`/`split_first`-style parsing with a non-digit port to assert on the resulting exception message, so this behavior change (and the same bug if reintroduced) would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: create_archive interpolates arguments into a shell string
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled with an f-string and executed with `shell=True`, so the two parameters are parsed by the shell rather than passed as argv entries. For plainly reachable inputs this is simply wrong: `create_archive("my report", "/data/logs")` becomes `tar -czf /exports/my report.tar.gz /data/logs`, which tars `report.tar.gz` and `/data/logs` into a file named `/exports/my` instead of producing the intended archive. Worse, a `name` or `directory` containing `;`, `&&`, `$(...)` or backticks executes attacker-chosen commands with the process's privileges — e.g. `directory="/data; rm -rf /exports"`.

Fix by passing an argument list and no shell, matching the sibling `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

If `name` is caller-supplied, also reject path separators and `..` so the output cannot escape `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection: f-string interpolated into subprocess with shell=True

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test exercising this function, so a change in its behavior (e.g. broken interpolation, wrong archive path, or command injection via crafted `name`/`directory`) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: dashboardCors sets origin "*" with credentials, removing the origin allowlist
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` replaces the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing middleware (line 6) with `origin: "*"`. Any route this middleware is mounted on becomes readable cross-origin by any website: a page the victim visits issues `fetch("https://api.../<route>")` and, because `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is returned, JavaScript on that page can read the response body. For an API reachable from the victim's network (corporate intranet, localhost dev/admin surfaces) this turns a blind CSRF into full response disclosure, and it also bypasses any authorisation that relied on the request coming from a known origin.

Separately, this will not achieve the stated goal. Browsers reject a credentialed request whose response carries a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so cookie-bearing dashboard calls will fail. The fix is the same in both cases: name the dashboard origin explicitly, e.g. `cors({ origin: [...ALLOWED, "https://dashboard.example.com"], credentials: true })`, or a function that validates the request `Origin` against an allowlist before reflecting it. Do not reflect `req.headers.origin` unconditionally as a workaround — that is equivalent to the wildcard but *also* works with cookies.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true cannot work for cookie requests
findings.body:
The stated goal is to let the dashboard origin call the API *with cookies*. This configuration cannot achieve that: when a request carries credentials, the browser requires a concrete, echoed `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value and rejects the literal `*`, so every credentialed dashboard request will still be blocked at the CORS check and `credentials: true` becomes dead configuration.

Replace the wildcard with the dashboard's concrete origin (or a reflect-from-allowlist function, as the existing export at lines 6-7 appears to do with `ALLOWED`), e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGIN` or `origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, ALLOWED.includes(o))`.

Note the alternative outcome is worse, not better: if the middleware here reflects the request origin instead of emitting a literal `*`, then any site on the internet can make authenticated, cookie-bearing calls and read the responses. Either the feature is broken or the origin check is effectively switched off — worth resolving explicitly before merge.

findings.title: No test coverage for new dashboardCors export
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers will refuse to honor credentialed requests with a wildcard origin). There is no test in this diff verifying the actual behavior of this exported middleware (e.g., asserting response headers on a request), so if this configuration is later 'fixed' incorrectly, or if the wildcard+credentials combination silently breaks the dashboard's cross-origin cookie auth, nothing would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` is a production payment-provider credential committed into the repository, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is removed in the same hunk). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a live-mode key, not a test key.

Impact: anyone with read access to the repo — every contributor, anyone with a clone, CI log scrapers, and anyone who ever gets a copy of the source or a built artifact — can authenticate to AcmePay as this account and issue charges, refunds, or read customer/payment data. The credential is also now in git history, so deleting the line in a follow-up commit does not remediate it.

Actions: (1) revoke/rotate this key in the AcmePay dashboard immediately, treat it as compromised; (2) restore the environment-variable (or secret-manager) lookup; (3) purge the value from git history or, more practically, rely on rotation since the old key becomes useless once revoked.

findings.title: Live key hardcoded removes per-environment configuration
findings.body:
`client()` previously resolved the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (local, CI, staging, production) supplied its own credential and a missing variable failed loudly. After this change every process that imports this module — including test runs and developer machines — authenticates with the `acme_live_...` key, so any code path that reaches a charge will move real money against the production account rather than a sandbox. The `import os` removal means there is no longer any way to override it without editing source.

Restore the environment lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) so the credential is per-environment, and rotate the key that has now been committed.

findings.title: Fixture return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, so callers use it as `client().charge(...)` or similar attribute access. `fake_client()` returns a plain `dict`, which supports neither attribute access nor the module's methods. If this fixture is monkeypatched in for `client`, the test will fail with `AttributeError` rather than exercising the code under test; if it is only used to assert on the configured key, it asserts against a value the production code no longer reads. Consider returning a stub object that mirrors the module's surface (e.g. a `SimpleNamespace` or a mock with `api_key` and the methods used).

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified JWT for tenant identity
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the payload is never checked against `public_key()`. Any caller using this to scope data access will accept a tenant id that the client can set freely by editing the token body — no signing key needed. Decode through the verified path (e.g. reuse `claims_for(token)` on line 6-7 and read `["tenant_id"]` from the result) rather than introducing a second, unverified decode. If the goal was to avoid the key-store round trip, cache the public key instead of dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test coverage for tenant_of() reading unverified claims
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the JWT with verify_signature=False and returns the tenant_id claim directly. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change that broke it (e.g. picking the wrong claim key, or a downstream authorization bypass introduced later) would not be caught. Given this function extracts a security-relevant claim (tenant id) without verification, at minimum a test should assert it returns the correct tenant_id for a given token and documents/enforces the intentional lack of signature verification.

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent
findings.body: A token without a `tenant_id` claim — which is entirely reachable since nothing here validates the payload shape — makes line 12 raise a bare `KeyError` rather than an auth error the callers can classify. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the project's auth exception, so callers do not surface a 500 for a malformed token.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates any user's card without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then saves \u2014 with no `require_owner(user, pm)` call. The attacker is any authenticated user of the API; what they control is the `pm_id` path/route parameter and the request body; what they get is the ability to overwrite the billing name on any other user's stored payment method (and, since the handler returns `pm.to_dict()`, to read back that record's fields, disclosing another user's payment details).

The adjacent read handler on line 6 already does the right thing, and `require_owner`'s own docstring states "Every object mutation must call this." Add the check immediately after the fetch:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

Note that `user` is currently bound on line 11 and never used, which is itself the tell that the authorisation call was dropped.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, missing authz would go unnoticed
findings.body: update_payment_method is added with no accompanying test. Unlike the neighboring function (line 6), it never calls require_owner(user, pm), so any signed-in user could update any other user's payment method. Because there is no test exercising this function — e.g. asserting that a non-owner request raises Forbidden — this defect would ship undetected. A test asserting ownership enforcement (mirroring how get_payment_method's require_owner path should be tested) is needed here.

findings.title: Public API contract undocumented and misleading
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint (line 10) that modifies user data but has no docstring. Worse, its implementation contradicts the repo's established contract: the `require_owner` function at line 7 of auth.py explicitly documents that "Every object mutation must call this," and the `get_payment_method` function above (lines 5-7) demonstrates the house style by calling `require_owner`. This function violates that contract without documenting why it is an exception. A caller reading the codebase would expect this function to check ownership, and the absence of a docstring explaining the authorization model makes this a public contract defect.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is reachable without authentication and now has no per-caller limit. An unauthenticated remote attacker who supplies an arbitrary `email` can call it in a loop to (a) flood a chosen victim's inbox with reset mails, a classic mail-bombing / social-engineering setup, (b) enumerate which addresses are registered by timing or observing response differences at scale, and (c) burn the sending domain's provider quota and reputation, which degrades reset mail for every user.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider throttling is applied per sending account or per originating domain, not per recipient and not per client IP, so it caps your own total send volume (turning the abuse into a denial of service against legitimate resets) rather than stopping a single attacker from targeting one victim or scanning the user table.

If the decorator must go, replace it with an equivalent limit keyed on both client IP and the target email address before merging, or keep `@rate_limit("5/hour")`.

findings.title: Password reset loses its only per-caller throttle
findings.body: `request_reset` now calls `send_reset_email` unconditionally with no limiter in front of it, so a single caller can drive an unbounded number of reset mails at any address. The stated justification — that the email provider throttles — does not cover this case: provider-side throttling is global to the sending account, not per target address or per requester, so it will not stop repeated resets aimed at one victim, and when it does trip it degrades delivery for every other transactional mail. If the limiter is genuinely redundant, replace it with an explicit per-email/per-IP check rather than removing the control outright; otherwise restore the decorator.

findings.title: Removal of rate limiting on reset endpoint has no accompanying test change
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, changing its throttling behavior. No test file is included in this PR, so if a test previously asserted that repeated calls to `request_reset` were throttled (e.g., returning an error or being blocked after N calls), that test would now need to be updated or removed, and if such a test doesn't exist, nothing in the suite would catch a regression if the limiter is reinstated incorrectly or removed by mistake in the future.

findings.title: Preview path bypasses _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The download path on line 14 resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead calls `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` yields a path outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", which is exactly the invariant that is broken here. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one enforcement point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function name does not convey path traversal risk
findings.body: `read_export_preview` has a name that mirrors the pattern of `read_export_file` (line 13), suggesting equivalent safety guarantees. However, it does not call `_confined()` to restrict the `name` parameter to the export directory, whereas `read_export_file` does on line 14. A caller reading only the function signature and name would reasonably assume both functions are equally safe to use with untrusted input, but `read_export_preview` permits path traversal attacks. Either confine the path using `_confined(name)` before line 20, or rename the function to make the lack of confinement explicit (e.g., `read_export_file_unchecked`).

findings.title: No test exercises read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the existing download path which calls _confined(name) (line 14). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression where 'name' contains '../' segments or an absolute path, nor would anything verify the preview correctly truncates to 'limit' bytes. Add a test asserting that a traversal-style name is rejected/confined the same way the download path is, and a test asserting the byte-limit behavior.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export leaks other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it with no tenant check. The removed loop was the only thing binding the requested objects to `current_user(request)`; `Report.get(rid)` is a direct lookup by ID, so the caller fully controls which rows are returned.

Adversary: any authenticated user (or any tenant, in a multi-tenant deployment). Controls: the `report_ids` list in the request. Gets: the full `to_dict()` contents of arbitrary reports belonging to other tenants, in bulk, by enumerating or guessing IDs.

Authentication is not authorisation — `current_user(request)` only establishes who is calling, not what they may read. Restore the check. If the per-object loop was the performance problem, push the constraint into the query instead of dropping it, e.g. fetch with `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and raise/404 when the returned count differs from the requested count (so a non-owned ID is not silently omitted in a way that leaks existence differently than intended).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer checks report ownership (cross-tenant read)

findings.title: Public endpoint no longer enforces documented auth contract
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function retrieves Report objects (line 6) without calling `require_owner` to enforce the documented authorization rule. The docstring in api/auth.py states: 'Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this', establishing a contract that callers can rely on. Removing the authorization check violates this contract without updating the documentation. A caller reading the contract would reasonably expect this endpoint to be safe to expose to authenticated users. Either restore the authorization check or update the `require_owner` docstring to document the exception for bulk operations.

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export's cross-tenant access control
findings.body: The diff removes the per-object `require_owner` check from `bulk_export`, meaning a user could now fetch reports belonging to another tenant simply by supplying arbitrary `report_ids`. No test file is included in this PR, and no existing test is visible in the retrieved context that exercises `bulk_export` with a report owned by a different tenant. If such a test existed and asserted a `Forbidden` exception on cross-tenant access, it would have failed on this change and caught the regression; since none is shown, nothing in the test suite would catch this behavior change.

findings.title: Unknown report ids now surface as a crash in to_dict()
findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an id that does not exist, `r.to_dict()` on line 7 raises `AttributeError` and the request fails with a 500 rather than a 404/400. Previously the deleted loop would at least have failed earlier (inside `require_owner`) for the same input, so this is not a regression introduced here, but whatever replaces the ownership check is the right place to handle missing ids explicitly — a tenant-scoped `id__in` query naturally returns fewer rows than requested, and the code should decide whether that is an error or a silent omission.

findings.title: execute() called without params, bypassing its parameterised contract
findings.body: `billing.db.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows it by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so caller-supplied values reach the driver as SQL text rather than bound parameters. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`term` and `status` are interpolated directly into the SQL string and the query is then handed to `execute(sql)` with no `params`, so the database driver never escapes them. A caller-supplied value such as `' OR '1'='1' -- ` in `status` returns the full customers table; `'; DROP TABLE customers; -- ` or a UNION payload in `term` extends the injection to arbitrary statements or cross-table reads, depending on driver multi-statement settings.

Fix by keeping the values out of the SQL text, matching `get_customer` on line 5 and the contract documented in `billing/db.py`:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the parameter value, not in the SQL literal.

findings.title: search_customers has no test covering its query construction
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL by interpolating `term` and `status` directly into the string (line 9) rather than using the parameterised `execute(sql, params)` pattern used by get_customer (line 5) and documented in billing/db.py. There is no test exercising this function, so a change that broke escaping, introduced injection, or altered the WHERE clause logic would pass silently. A test asserting the SQL string/params passed to execute (or an integration test with special characters in term/status) would catch this.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes the URL straight to `requests.get` with no validation, while the delivery path a few lines above rejects any destination whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9). The allowlist that protects the POST path is simply not applied on this new GET path.

Adversary: any tenant who can register or test a webhook target. What they control: the full URL, including scheme, host and port. What they get: the service makes an outbound request from inside your network and returns the HTTP status code, giving a working oracle for internal port/host scanning (`http://10.0.0.5:8080/`), for hitting unauthenticated internal admin endpoints, and for cloud instance metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`). `file://` may also be accepted depending on the installed adapters.

Fix: run the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used by the delivery function before issuing the request — ideally factored into a shared `_check_destination(url)` helper so the two paths cannot drift again. Also resolve the host and reject private/link-local/loopback address ranges, restrict the scheme to https, and pass `allow_redirects=False`, since `requests` follows redirects by default and a 302 to an internal address would defeat a hostname-only allowlist.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ verify_endpoint has no test and skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code will, for the most common failure it exists to detect (DNS failure, refused connection, or the 5s timeout firing), raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than returning anything. Callers registering a tenant webhook will almost certainly treat this as "return a status I can compare" and will get an unhandled exception on the exact input they were trying to validate. Wrap the call and return a sentinel (or `None`) on `RequestException`, or document that it raises so callers handle it.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
